meta.title: Who really said "Work is love made visible"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Kahlil Gibran wrote it. The line lands near the end of "On Work" in The Prophet (Knopf, 1923), confirmed in the 1923 text. Popular versions reword it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Work is love made visible'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Gibran wrote it in English for The Prophet, published 23 September 1923. But the original reads "cannot," not "can't" — and the warning that follows is usually cut.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence appears in the closing movement of “On Work,” one of the twenty-six prose-poem chapters of The Prophet, published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York on 23 September 1923. Gibran wrote The Prophet in English, so there is no translation standing between him and the wording — the four words are his own, confirmed against the 1923 text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 23 September 1923 · Alfred A. Knopf, New York
Written in English — not a translation

source.excerpt:
And he alone is great who turns the voice of the wind into a song made sweeter by his own loving.

Work is love made visible.

And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste, it is better that you should leave your work and sit at the gate of the temple and take alms of those who work with joy.
trail: Searched Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote’s Gibran page ↗ first. Neither has investigated this line — and notably, Wikiquote does not list it among the quotes misattributed to him. With no specialist finding to defer to, the check went straight to the book.
Located the sentence in Project Gutenberg’s text of The Prophet ↗ (Knopf, 1923), which the site marks public domain in the USA. It appears as its own line in “On Work.”

Cross-checked the wording and its position against an independent full text of the chapter at poets.org ↗, which credits The Prophet (Knopf, 1923). Both agree the sentence follows “…a song made sweeter by his own loving” and precedes “And if you cannot work with love…”

Dated the first publication to 23 September 1923 via Princeton University Library’s Manuscripts Division ↗, and confirmed with Wikipedia ↗ that Gibran composed the book in English, so the wording is his and not a translator’s.

source.rightsNote: The Prophet was first published in the United States on 23 September 1923, and works published in 1923 entered the US public domain on 1 January 2019 — which is why Project Gutenberg ↗ hosts the complete text and marks it “public domain in the USA.” Because Gibran wrote the book in English, there is no separate translation copyright to consider. Wikipedia ↗ records that the Gibran National Committee, founded in 1935, manages Gibran’s copyrights; that does not affect the US public-domain status of the 1923 text, though rights in other jurisdictions and in later material may differ.

author.name: Kahlil Gibran
author.heading: Who was Kahlil Gibran?
author.metaLine: 1883–1931 · Lebanese-American poet, painter and author of The Prophet
author.bio: Born in Bsharri, in what was then the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate of the Ottoman Empire, Gibran emigrated to Boston as a child and was registered in America under the anglicized spelling Kahlil — his Arabic name was Jubrān Khalīl Jubrān. He worked as both a writer and a visual artist, and the twelve illustrations in The Prophet are reproduced from his own drawings. He died in New York City on 10 April 1931; The Prophet, published eight years earlier, remains the book his name is attached to.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right — the quotation isn't
misattribution.intro: Gibran is one of the internet’s great magnets for invented quotations, so the first question is whether this one is real. It is. The problems here are of a different kind: the wording drifts, and the sentence is almost always cut loose from the condition that gives it force.

items.why: A widely-shared version reads “And if you can’t work with love… take alms of the people who work with joy” — as it appears on Goodreads ↗. The 1923 text reads “cannot” and “those who work with joy.”

The four words are nearly always quoted alone, which turns a warning into a compliment. In the full chapter ↗ the very next sentence tells the reader who cannot work with love to leave the work altogether. Reading the line as praise for hard work inverts what Gibran is arguing.

Gibran attracts fabrications freely: Wikiquote ↗ catalogues lines circulating under his name that belong to Chapin or to no traceable source at all. That record is why a Gibran quotation deserves checking — and why it is worth saying plainly that this one survives the check.

Both spellings appear on reprints and quote sites. Wikipedia ↗ notes his Arabic name was Jubrān Khalīl Jubrān, anglicized to “Kahlil Gibran” when it was registered in America; a later American sculptor bore the same name.

misattribution.truthLine: Gibran wrote it, in English, and it was printed in The Prophet in 1923 ↗. Quote it as “cannot,” and if you have room, keep the sentence that follows it.

context.heading: Why the sentence has teeth
lead: Lifted onto a poster, “Work is love made visible” reads as pure affirmation — a compliment paid to effort. In the book it is nothing so comfortable. It is the hinge of an argument, and the very next line turns it into a test: “And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste, it is better that you should leave your work and sit at the gate of the temple and take alms of those who work with joy.”

Gibran builds to it carefully. Earlier in the chapter he defines what working with love actually means — weaving cloth with threads drawn from your heart, building a house with affection, sowing seeds with tenderness, “as if your beloved were to eat the fruit.” Then he presses the point in the negative: bread baked with indifference is bitter bread, and a grudge held while crushing the grapes “distils a poison in the wine.” If work makes love visible, then joyless work makes its absence visible too. That is the half of the passage that rarely survives the quotation.
detailsBody: “On Work” moves in stages. It opens by tying labour to life itself — “And in keeping yourself with labour you are in truth loving life” — then answers the question “And what is it to work with love?” with a series of images of craft performed as if for a beloved.

Gibran then rejects a hierarchy of trades: he quotes the common view that he who works in marble “is nobler than he who ploughs the soil,” and refuses it, saying the wind “speaks not more sweetly to the giant oaks than to the least of all the blades of grass.” Only after levelling the crafts does he land the famous sentence — which is why it reads as a conclusion rather than a slogan.
The chapter then closes on three warnings, about indifferent bread, grudged grapes and loveless singing, ending: “you muffle man’s ears to the voices of the day and the voices of the night.”
context.pull: And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste, it is better that you should leave your work…

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg's edition of The Prophet (Kahlil Gibran, New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1923) contains the line "Work is love made visible." in the chapter on Work, immediately followed by "And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste, it is better that you should leave your work and sit at the gate of the temple and take alms of those who work with joy."
Project Gutenberg ebook #58585 is The Prophet by Kahlil Gibran (1883-1931), released 1 January 2019, and is explicitly marked "Public domain in the USA."

An independent full text of The Prophet confirms the same wording and the same ordering: "...And he alone is great who turns the voice of the wind into a song made sweeter by his own loving. / Work is love made visible. And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste..."
The Academy of American Poets reproduces Gibran's "On Work" in full, containing "Work is love made visible," and credits it to The Prophet (Knopf, 1923), noting it is in the public domain.
The Internet Archive hosts a full-view scan of The Prophet published New York: A. A. Knopf, 1923, 107 pages.

Princeton University Library's Manuscripts Division states that classic works first published in 1923 entered the US public domain in 2019, and that Gibran's The Prophet was "first published by the New York publisher Alfred A. Knopf on 23 September 1923."
Wikipedia states The Prophet was written in English by Kahlil Gibran and published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1923, and notes the Gibran National Committee (founded 1935) manages Gibran's copyright.

Wikipedia gives Gibran's dates as born 6 January 1883 in Bsharri (Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate, Ottoman Empire) and died 10 April 1931 in New York City; states his Arabic name was Jubran Khalil Jubran, anglicized to "Kahlil Gibran" on registration in America; and references a Kahlil Gibran who was a sculptor.
Wikiquote's Khalil Gibran page lists quotes misattributed to Gibran, including one actually by Edwin Hubbell Chapin and one unattributable line popularized in August 2016.

NEGATIVE CHECK - Wikiquote's Khalil Gibran page does NOT contain "Work is love made visible" in any section, sourced or misattributed. The quote is therefore neither confirmed nor flagged there; verification rests on the primary text instead.

A widely-shared variant on Goodreads reads "Work is love made visible. And if you can't work with love, but only with distaste, it is better that you should leave your work and sit at the gate of the temple and take alms of the people who work with joy" - using "can't" rather than the original "cannot" and "the people who" rather than "those who."

NEGATIVE CHECK - no Quote Investigator article on "Work is love made visible" was found via site-restricted search; QI has not investigated this quotation, so there is no specialist anchor finding to defer to.
